title: How to Hand Off Support Conversations Between Shifts Without Losing Context
excerpt: A shift handoff routine for small DTC support teams: what every open ticket needs before it is passed on, decision limits for quiet hours, and the metric that proves it worked.
body: Support quality drops at the seams. Not because the team is careless, but because the moment one person stops and another starts is where context disappears. A customer explains a damaged shipment at six in the evening, writes again at nine the next morning, and gets asked the same three questions. For a small DTC team covering long hours, a real handoff routine is worth more than another tool. The DTCwise Customer Support category at /category/support keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing for teams building one.

Define what a closed handoff looks like before you write any rules. At the end of a shift, every open conversation should have three things attached: what the customer asked for, what has already been done, and what the next person needs to do and by when. If any of those are missing, the conversation stays open in a named queue rather than getting passed along. That single rule removes the most common failure, which is a ticket that looks handled and quietly is not.

Write the note for a stranger, not for yourself. Waiting on warehouse is useless at nine in the morning. Order one zero four two, mug arrived chipped, photo received, replacement approved, tracking number needs to go out before eleven is a note anyone can act on. Train the team to put the customer's request in the customer's words first, then add the internal decision. It costs twenty extra seconds per ticket and saves the next agent from rereading the entire thread.

Split queues by urgency rather than by channel. Live chat and email are different channels but the same work during a handoff, and what actually matters is whether something is about to break. Use three buckets: needs action today, waiting on a third party, and low priority. The incoming shift reads the first bucket first, every time, before opening the main inbox. Check /tool/tidio on DTCwise if you are evaluating live chat and shared inbox setups that keep these queues visible to a small team.

Give whoever covers the quiet hours a decision floor. The person watching overnight or weekend needs to know what they can resolve without waking anyone: reship up to a stated dollar amount, refund up to a stated dollar amount, issue store credit. Write the limits down. Without them, either nothing gets resolved until the next business day, or someone approves a refund that wipes out the margin on the order. Both are expensive, and both are avoidable with one paragraph of policy.

Make the handoff a written ritual rather than a verbal one. A shared note per shift with three lines: open tickets by bucket, anything escalated, anything a customer was promised. Five minutes at the end of each shift, read at the start of the next. Then measure it the way you measure everything else. First response time tells you about speed, but tickets reopened after being marked resolved tells you whether the handoff actually worked.
